chunks: Sample rate needed to measure a sine wave. The question: If I want to measure a sine wave, what should be the sample rate?
The textbook answer is that you must sample a sine wave at more than twice its frequency. That is only the theoretical minimum.
The rate you really need depends on what you want to measure: just the frequency, the shape of the wave, or its exact peak height.
Reading the peak straight from raw samples needs many more samples per cycle.
Suppose you take snapshots of a swinging playground swing. To know how fast it swings, a few photos per swing are enough. To see its path, you want more.
To know exactly how high it goes, you need a photo near the very top.
With only two photos per swing, you might always catch it passing through the middle and conclude it barely moves.
At exactly twice the frequency the data can look like a full-amplitude sine or like a flat line, depending only on when sampling starts.
Any rate strictly above 2f drifts through the phase and reveals the amplitude, which is why the theorem is stated with a strict inequality.
Sample rate: how many measurements are taken per second. Samples per cycle: the sample rate divided by the signal frequency.
Aliasing: a too-high frequency appearing as a lower one in the samples. Anti-alias filter: a filter before the converter that blocks frequencies that are too high.
Interpolation: filling in the values between samples, for example when a scope draws the wave.
Take a 1 kilohertz sine. Theory needs more than 2 kS/s (2000 samples per second). Now the raw peak.
With N samples per cycle, the nearest sample can miss the true peak, and in the worst case reads low by 1 minus cos(π ÷ N). With N = 10 (10 kS/s) the error is up to 4. 9%.
With N = 20 it is about 1. 2%. You need N = 23, so 23 kS/s, to stay under 1%.
An oscilloscope (a screen that draws signals) avoids this by interpolating, so 5 to 10 samples per cycle looks fine on screen.
Too slow is worse: a 900 hertz sine sampled at 1 kS/s looks like a 100 hertz sine. That is the whole idea.
"The Nyquist criterion says more than twice the signal frequency, so for a 1 kilohertz sine, over 2 kS/s.
That's the theoretical minimum, though: exactly 2 times can sample zero crossings, and real systems need an anti-alias filter, so I'd use about 2. 5 to 4 times .

For viewing a waveform on a scope I'd use 5 to 10 times with interpolation, and for peak amplitude from raw samples the worst-case error is 1 minus cosine of pi over N, so about 23 samples per cycle for under 1 percent."
